newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: World Court to decide Malaysia-Indonesia dispute.
newsitem.headline: World Court to decide Malaysia-Indonesia dispute.

text.p: Malaysia and Indonesia agreed on Monday to let the International Court of Justice decide who has sovereignty over two islands they both claim, Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas said.

Visiting Indonesian President Suharto and Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad agreed on Monday to let the world court in The Hague rule on who owns Sipadan and Ligitan, two small islands off the east coast of Borneo.

"This is one problem that should not be left too long unresolved because it could only be exploited by those who do not want see close relations between Indonesia and Malaysia," Alatas told reporters after a meeting between Suharto and Mahathir.
The two countries have tried unsuccessfully to resolve the issue for the past five years through diplomatic and political channels.

The two heads of government decided to refer the dispute to the world court because "both sides feel this should be resolved, and must be resolved, as soon as possible in the spirit of ASEAN," Alatas said.
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.

The decades-old dispute flared up in 1991 after Malaysia began promoting the islands as a tourist destination. Naval ships from both countries have been sent to the islands since then to stage exercises, but there have been no clashes.

Diplomats say the relatively friendly disagreement stands in contrast to the dispute involving Japan, China and Taiwan over the small East China Sea islands called the Senkakus in Japanese and the Diaoyus in Chinese.
China also is at odds with several countries in Southeast Asia over ownership of the Spratlys in the South China Sea.
But ASEAN has had some success mending disputes in its own backyard.
Malaysia and Singapore have already agreed to refer their overlapping claims to Batu Seputeh (White Rock) island in the South China Sea to the International Court of Justice.
Suharto left for home on Monday after a one-day visit that focussed mainly on economic matters.
